quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Repos, Staging, and Commits
quizzes.intro: Check core Git mental models before branching and collaboration.

questions.prompt: What is the staging area for?

options.text: Hosting the only copy of project history on GitHub
Preparing a selected set of changes for the next commit
Compiling code automatically
Deleting remote branches

questions.explanation: Staging lets you craft the exact snapshot that the next commit will record.

wrongExplanations.a: History lives in the repository; remotes are separate.
wrongExplanations.c: Git does not compile your application in the staging area.
wrongExplanations.d: Branch deletion is a different operation.

questions.prompt: Which command shows whether files are modified, staged, or untracked?

options.text: git paint
git status
git merge --abort --please
git password

questions.explanation: git status is the everyday dashboard for working tree and staging state.

wrongExplanations.a: That is not a Git command.
wrongExplanations.c: Merge abort is for stopping a merge, not routine status.
wrongExplanations.d: That is not how Git reports file state.

questions.prompt: What makes a strong commit message?

options.text: A vague label like "update" or "final"
A clear explanation of why the change exists, often in imperative style
A list of every keystroke you made
No message at all

questions.explanation: Useful messages communicate intent so history remains searchable and reviewable.

wrongExplanations.a: Vague messages hide intent and hurt debugging.
wrongExplanations.c: Commit messages summarize purpose; they are not keystroke logs.
wrongExplanations.d: Commits require messages for collaboration and clarity.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

options.text: They are identical products with different logos
Git is version control software; GitHub is a hosting/collaboration platform built around Git repos
GitHub replaces the need for commits
Git can only store images, while GitHub stores code

questions.explanation: Git works locally as VCS; GitHub adds remotes, PRs, issues, and team workflows.

wrongExplanations.a: They are related but not the same thing.
wrongExplanations.c: Commits remain central whether or not you use GitHub.
wrongExplanations.d: Both can store many file types; the distinction is not file-type based.

questions.prompt: Why inspect git diff before committing?

options.text: Because commits are impossible without printing diffs to paper
To review exact changes and catch accidental debug code, secrets, or unrelated edits
Because diff deletes remote history
Because diff renames the default branch

questions.explanation: Reading diffs is a professional safeguard before recording history.

wrongExplanations.a: Diff review is a habit, not a paper requirement.
wrongExplanations.c: git diff inspects changes; it does not delete remote history.
wrongExplanations.d: Branch renaming is a separate action.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Branches, Remotes, and Safety
quizzes.intro: Test branching, remotes, ignores, and undo judgment.

questions.prompt: What is a branch in Git?

options.text: A movable pointer to a commit used for parallel lines of work
A forced deletion of all history
A GUI-only label with no commit meaning
A replacement for commit messages

questions.explanation: Branches point at commits and let teams develop features in isolation.

wrongExplanations.b: Creating a branch does not delete history.
wrongExplanations.c: Branches are real Git references, not cosmetic GUI stickers.
wrongExplanations.d: Messages and branches solve different problems.

questions.prompt: What should you do if a secret API key appears in git status as a new file?

options.text: Commit it quickly so it is backed up
Stop, keep it out of the commit, add it to .gitignore, and protect/rotate credentials as needed
Rename the key file to README.md and commit
Push first, then decide later

questions.explanation: Secrets must not enter history; prevention and rotation beat cleanup.

wrongExplanations.a: Committing secrets is a security incident waiting to happen.
wrongExplanations.c: Renaming does not make a secret safe to commit.
wrongExplanations.d: Pushing spreads the problem to the remote.

questions.prompt: When is git revert generally safer than rewriting shared history?

options.text: When the commit was never created
When a bad commit is already shared and others may depend on it
When you want to delete Git from the computer
When you only need to view status

questions.explanation: Revert adds a new undoing commit and avoids disrupting collaborators who already pulled.

wrongExplanations.a: There is nothing to revert if no commit exists.
wrongExplanations.d: Status viewing does not require revert.

options.text: Downloads and applies remote commits only
Uploads local commits to a remote repository
Creates a .gitignore automatically
Resolves all merge conflicts magically

questions.explanation: Push publishes local commits to the configured remote branch.

wrongExplanations.c: Ignore files are created manually or by templates.

questions.prompt: Why do teams use feature branches instead of committing unfinished work directly to main?

options.text: Because main cannot store commits
To isolate in-progress work and keep the stable line cleaner until review/integration
Because GitHub rejects all commits to any branch named main
Because branches disable git status

questions.explanation: Feature branches separate experiments and unfinished work from the shared stable branch.

wrongExplanations.a: main stores commits like any branch.
wrongExplanations.c: GitHub does not universally reject main commits; protections are configurable.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Pull Requests, Conflicts, and Collaboration
quizzes.intro: Apply GitHub collaboration habits and conflict judgment.

questions.prompt: What is a pull request primarily for?

options.text: Proposing that one branch be merged into another with discussion and review
Deleting the remote permanently
Replacing the need for commits
Formatting CSS only

questions.explanation: PRs are the collaboration unit for reviewing and integrating branch work.

wrongExplanations.b: PRs integrate changes; they are not remote deletion tools.
wrongExplanations.c: Commits still form the history inside the PR.
wrongExplanations.d: PRs can include any project files, not only CSS.

questions.prompt: A merge conflict appears. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore marker lines and push anyway
Edit the file to the intended final content, remove conflict markers, stage, and complete the merge
Delete the repository and start without Git
Assume Git chose correctly and never open the file

questions.explanation: Conflicts require human judgment to produce the correct combined result.

wrongExplanations.a: Leaving markers breaks code and documents.
wrongExplanations.c: Conflicts are normal and solvable without abandoning Git.
wrongExplanations.d: Git stops precisely because it cannot choose safely.

questions.prompt: Which quality most improves a pull request for reviewers?

options.text: Mixing unrelated refactors, features, and formatting in one giant diff
A focused change with a clear summary and test notes
No title and no description
Force-pushing every minute without explanation

questions.explanation: Reviewers need a coherent story and a manageable diff to give useful feedback.

wrongExplanations.a: Kitchen-sink PRs hide bugs and exhaust reviewers.
wrongExplanations.c: Context is essential for review quality.
wrongExplanations.d: Noisy history updates without communication hurt collaboration.

questions.prompt: Why keep node_modules out of Git with .gitignore in typical JS projects?

options.text: Because dependencies can be restored from package manifests and bloating history hurts the repo
Because Git cannot store folders
Because GitHub bans all JavaScript
Because ignored files can never be created locally

questions.explanation: Dependencies are reinstallable; committing them creates huge, noisy repositories.

wrongExplanations.b: Git can store folders/files; ignoring is a choice.
wrongExplanations.c: JavaScript projects are extremely common on GitHub.
wrongExplanations.d: Ignored files can exist locally; they are simply untracked.

questions.prompt: Before experimenting with an unfamiliar undo command, what is a safe habit?

options.text: Run reset --hard on main immediately
Create a backup branch or otherwise ensure you can recover, especially if work matters
Delete .git to simplify things
Disable git status forever

questions.explanation: A safety branch preserves a recoverable pointer before risky experiments.

wrongExplanations.a: Hard resets on shared branches can destroy work.
wrongExplanations.d: Status is a core safety tool.

questions.prompt: A command completes without error after a merge. What does that guarantee?

options.text: The product behavior is definitely correct
Only that Git could complete the operation—not that the combined code meets product intent
All reviewers approved the change
No tests are needed ever again

questions.explanation: Git success means history operations finished; quality still needs human and automated verification.

wrongExplanations.a: Merged code can still be logically wrong.
wrongExplanations.c: Command success is unrelated to review approvals.
